gloss: Abdiel. *champain*, plains.
Homer makes the Hours keep the gates of Olympus. *with rosy hand*; “rosy-fingered” became in poetry a traditional epithet of the dawn.

The notion of light and darkness “dislodging by turns,” the one going out as the other comes in, had its origin in Hesiod, *Theogony* 747, 748 (Newton). *vicissitude*, alternation. *Obsequious*, obedient, doing its duty; not in the modern depreciatory sense, ‘servile.’
ready. “The Roman soldiers were said to stand *in procinctu*, when ready to give the onset” (Hume).

Is Milton here thinking of himself? He too had sacrificed all to “the testimony of truth” (as he judged), and borne reproach for his allegiance to the cause of republicanism when the “revolted multitudes” went back to the old order of things and acclaimed the Restoration.

M. seems to use the phrase = ‘conscience’; cf. *The Christian Doctrine*, I. 2, “that feeling, whether we term it conscience or right reason.” It was a term of the Stoics, reproduced in the Schoolmen’s phrase *recta ratio*.
Michael, ‘who is like unto God?’; being an archangel he is chosen to fulfil high office. *Gabriel*; he is inferior to Michael (“next,” 45) because only an angel.
i.e. smoke began to roll flames in wreaths. *reluctant*, struggling, forcing their way through the smoke; a Latinism.
i.e. began. But wherever he uses *gan*, ‘beginning’ is implied.
A simile that would appeal to Adam. “And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field,” Gen. ii. 20.
M. clearly places the conflict in some part of Heaven; but this was a point much disputed among theologians.

i.e. and at nearer view there bristled the banded powers. *bristled*; this seems to be the main verb; it conveys the same impression as Lat. *horrere*. *beams*, shafts of the spears. *argument*, designs, subjects; a Latinism.
*Idol*, image. *flaming Cherubim*; M. always invests the Cherubim with brilliance, following Ezekiel.
i.e. the van-guard (Fr. *avant-garde*) dense as a cloud. *edge*, Lat. *acies*, the front line of a fight.
reality. What Abdiel deplores is that Satan retains the outward semblance of greatness after the inward reality has gone from him.
coming before; the lit. sense of Lat. *praevenire*. *securely*, without anxiety, boldly—Lat. *secure*.

*sect*, followers (Lat. *sequi*); in modern E. depreciatory. M. may have brought in the word ironically, “in order to sneer at the Loyalists of his time, who branded all Dissenters, of whom he was one, with the opprobrious name of Sectaries” (Thyer).
M. is glancing at one of his favourite maxims, that too many men had rather purchase ease at the expense of slavery than liberty at the cost of effort.

A contemptuous jingle; both words are from Lat. *minister*. There is a reference to Hebrews i. 14, “Are they not all ministering spirits?” *minstrelsy*, minstrels; *servility*, slaves; *freedom*, free men.
The idea that earthquakes were due to the escape of winds pent up underground comes in Dante (*Purgatorio*, XXI. 55, 56).
In the description that follows editors find echoes of Hesiod’s account of the strife between the Titans and Zeus.

“Each legion was in number like an army, each single warriour was in strength like a legion, and, though led in fight, was as expert as a commander in chief” (Newton). *numbered such*, so numerous. *ridges*, i.e. the ranks of troops.
*moment*, the impulse that should turn the scale on the side of victory; Lat. *momentum*.

Cf. the sword of Æneas and King Arthur’s mystic Excalibur in the *Idylls of the King*. Supernatural equipment of the hero is an epic convention. *two-handed*, i.e. wielded with both hands because of its size and weight.

lemma: if to fall, but that they rise
gloss: i.e. even if they have fallen, yet they have risen again. ‘Have you,’ says Satan, ‘been so successful in putting these to flight, that you should hope to deal (“transact”) easily with me?’
i.e. such commotion as there would be, if, nature’s concord having been broken, war should arise among the constellations, and two planets should combat.

*aspect*; in Elizabethan E. often used as an astrological term signifying the position of a planet in the sky, and its “influence,” which was favourable or “malign” according to its position. When two planets are in diametrically opposite parts of the heavens, they are said to be “in opposition.”
“The Lord hath opened his armoury,” Jeremiah l. 25.

Only the rebellious angels are sensible of physical pain. Through sin they have made gross the pure “essence” of their original forms; and spirit has deteriorated into matter, rendering them vulnerable. The obedient angels are invulnerable because innocent.
*griding*, piercing, cutting through. “Discontinuous wound is said in allusion to the old definition of a wound, that it separates the continuity of the parts” (Newton).
i.e. the “essence” of which he speaks in I. 424, 425—“soft and uncompounded.” *no more than can the fluid air*. A favourite poetic comparison.

With regard to some of the names here and later we have seen that M. adopted the mediaeval notion that the deities of heathenism, oriental and classical, were the apostate angels. He could not describe their rebellion without giving them some titles: this belief supplied him with suitable names.
Moloch illustrates his character in his speech in II. 51–105: his “ferocious character,” says Johnson, “appears, both in the battle and the council, with exact consistency.”

*Adramelech*, ‘magnificence of the king’; a deity whose worship was brought to Samaria by the colonists from Sepharvaim (2 Kings xvii. 31). *Asmadai*; see IV. 168, where M. uses the form Asmodeus. In the systems of demonology popular in the 16th and 17th centuries Asmodeus held very high rank, and was a type of might.

*Ariel*, ‘lion of God.’ Probably M. has used the name merely because its meaning is so descriptive of a great warrior. *Arioch*, ‘lion-like.’ *Ramiel*, ‘exaltation of God.’ “Milton’s proper names are often chosen for their full sounds” (Tennyson).
*cubic*, four-square; not an exact use of the word, but editors compare Milton’s *Reason of Church Government*, “as those smaller squares in battle unite in one great cube, the main phalanx.”
an old ballad-phrase. It occurs in *Henry V*, IV. 6. 18. It is one of the old-world phrases revived by Tennyson.
the Assyrian deity in whose temple Sennacherib was murdered by his sons, 2 Kings xix. 37, Isaiah xxxvii. 38. Probably it means ‘great eagle.’
A sentiment “suitable enough to a deity of the effeminate Assyrians” (Newton). In the reference to “pain” there may be a personal glance.
Editors show that the notion that cannon were invented in Hell is found in Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*, IX. 28, *The Faerie Queene*, I. 7. 13, and Drayton’s *Polyolbion*, 18.
*cheer*, spirits; generally high spirits, joy, but not always. Properly *cheer* means face, and some editors think that it has that sense here.
Adam’s. Probably M. is thinking of the Civil War. Descriptions of civil strife and its incidents must have appealed with the force of personal experience to many of his readers.
*engines*, i.e. cannon. When cannon were first used, the balls were made of stone, not iron. *incentive reed*, i.e. the gunner’s match. *incentive*, enkindling.
i.e. the swiftest-winged Cherub. Zophiel, ‘spy of God.’ M. seems to have invented the name—appropriately, since the Cherub is one of the scouts sent out (529).
i.e. arrows with fire at their points. A barb is a hook or jag on an arrow-head.

The irony and verbal quibbles—“discharge,” “touch,” etc.—are too obvious to need comment. Humour is not Milton’s forte. Addison considered this part “the most exceptionable in the whole poem,” on account of these quibbles.

lemma: A triple mounted row of pillars
gloss: The sense appears to be: ‘We saw a row of brazen or iron pillars—at least things which but for their hollow mouths we should have supposed to be pillars.’ *hollow*, i.e. deceitful, as applied to “truce”; but there is a quibbling reference to the hollow barrels of the guns.
M. attributes to spiritual beings the power of reducing or expanding (“dilating,” I. 429) themselves at will.

Newton notes that the speech is appropriate to the character of Belial as drawn in the first two books of the poem. There Belial was described as a god of the unwarlike, and here, in the great battle, “we find him celebrated for nothing but that scoffing speech” (Addison).
Vergil’s *furor arma ministrat*, *Æn.* I. 150.
Lat. *jaculatio*, ‘a casting, hurling.’ Addison compares the classical legends about Pelion and Ossa in the Giants’ war.
i.e. in whose face that which is invisible—namely, what I by Deity am—is visibly beheld. Cf. Colos. i. 15, “Who is the image of the invisible God.”
*suspend*, delay. The sense is—‘Though sin has done them some harm, yet it has not made them so inferior to the good angels that the latter can win a decisive victory.’
the whole “continent” (474) of Heaven, or the whole Universe.
*utter*, outer.
“Milton, by continuing the war for three days, and reserving the victory upon the third for the Messiah alone, plainly alludes to the circumstances of his death and resurrection” (Newton).

This description of the throne-chariot of the Deity, and of the Cherubic Shapes whereby it was convoyed, is modelled very closely on Ezekiel’s Vision, chap. i. *Paradise Lost* contains no more striking instance of his skill in adapting Scripture to the purposes of his work.

Concerning the much-discussed Urim, it seems to be agreed that they were certain material objects placed inside the breastplate of judgment which formed part of the high priest’s ephod. The general sense is—‘armed in celestial equipment wrought of precious stones.’
“And he rode upon a cherub and did fly,” 2 Sam. xxii. 11. M. generally uses *sublime* = Lat. *sublimis* in its literal sense, ‘uplifted.’
senseless.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord,” Romans xii. 19.
This description recalls *An Apology for Smectymnuus*: “then Zeal, whose substance is ethereal, arming in complete diamond, ascends his fiery chariot, drawn with two blazing meteors.”
“And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the wrath of the Lamb,” Rev. vi. 16. The irony of the lines, in view of 639–66, is obvious.
The “bottomless pit” is the lowest region of Hell—that “fiery gulf” on which the angels are depicted as tossing in I. 52.
a symbol of victory. *sung triumph*; M. is thinking perhaps of the Lat. *Io Triumphe*, the cry raised by the crowd and soldiers when a Roman general celebrated his triumph.

lemma: he who envies now thy state
gloss: These lines give the two main motives of Satan’s resolve to ruin mankind, namely, envy and desire to spite God by marring his creatures: man shall be ruined that Satan may be revenged on the Most High for his defeat.
It is the sentiment expressed in the proverbial line of unknown origin, *solamen miseris socios habuisse doloris*.
Eve, “the weaker vessel,” 1 Pet. iii. 7.
